items.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: maybe he’ll discover Rudy Weidoft instead of Charlie Parker.

ctx.x: before young people of their own volition sit down one day, go to a library, pick up a Charlie Parker record and now you’ve got to let them think it’s their discovery, “I’ve discovered Charlie Parker.” When they think it’s their discovery and they think it’s their peer group way of being hip, then I think quality will kind of reinvent itself and become part of the scenario like you said.

Well I hope that this is true, not only for your sake, but for all of our sakes, and for people who live music and practitioners and artists, you know who have come to the height of a Charlie Parker phenomenon. But that type of phenomenon needs to be nurtured in a culture that digs what it is doing. And just, although jazz music was always a minor, I mean a subculture, a minor percentage of the population really knew — I mean the so-called jazz age was not the jazz age at all. Big bands were not jazz music. Great…
Yeah, I do see what you’re saying.

items.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Rudy Weidoft’s brother was supposedly a trumpet player. And it is a gorgeous tune. And that’s what I remember, sort of.

ctx.x: So they were still doing the two beat kind of thing.

Sure. I think one of the big hits of the day, because I remember my mother singing this, was “Lookie, Lookie, Lookie, Here Comes Cookie.” And then there was a very good film which grabbed me later on in life which had George Raft playing a good guy as a band leader wearing a white jacket called “Every Night at Eight” or something like that, and Frances Langford was the girl singer with the band and she sang this one tune “And You’ve Never Been Blue,” which is really a wonderful tune you know. And it’s sort of…
What put a clarinet in your hands as a young kid?
